Sector Case Study · IT Services

Indian IT Services: Studying Operating Margins, Deal Mix and Cash Conversion

An educational case study demonstrating how analysts compare employee utilization, attrition, subcontracting costs, and free-cash-flow conversion across large-cap and mid-cap Indian IT services companies.

  • Document ClassificationEducational case study / learning report (mentor-reviewed)
  • AuthorHarion Research Learning Lab (Mentor-Reviewed Sample)
  • Published Date2026-10-15
  • Positions DisclosedNo position disclosed. Prepared strictly as an educational template.
Educational Notice: This report is prepared solely as an academic and analytical case study demonstrating financial research methodology. It contains no target price, no buy/sell/hold rating, and is not investment advice.

1. Purpose of this learning report

This educational case study illustrates how participants in the Harion Equity Research Internship Program structure a sector-level financial comparison. Rather than forecasting share prices or issuing recommendations, a sector study begins by identifying the core operating drivers that explain why two companies in the same industry earn different returns on capital.

2. Business model & revenue drivers

Indian IT services companies generate revenue primarily through time-and-materials (T&M) and fixed-price contracts across banking, retail, manufacturing, and healthcare verticals. When reading annual reports in this sector, analysts track billable headcount, offshore-to-onsite revenue mix, client concentration buckets ($10M+, $50M+, $100M+ accounts), and constant-currency revenue growth.

3. Financial statement & ratio comparison

In the Harion Research Scanner, IT services firms frequently screen with low balance-sheet leverage (minimal Debt-to-Equity) and high Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) because physical capital intensity is low. The analytical differentiator lies in Operating Profit Margin (OPM %) stability and the ratio of Operating Cash Flow (OCF) to EBITDA, which reveals how effectively billed revenue converts into cash after working-capital changes (unbilled receivables and debtor days).

4. Valuation context & historical multiples

Analysts compare trailing Price-to-Earnings (P/E) and EV/EBITDA multiples against 5-year historical medians and against reported revenue growth rates. A higher multiple in historical data often reflects lower client concentration risk and higher cash payout ratios (dividends and buybacks), whereas compressed multiples frequently coincide with margin headwinds or vertical-specific slowdowns.

5. Key risks & analytical limitations

Key variables that can alter historical trajectories include foreign-exchange fluctuations (USD/INR, EUR/INR), visa and onsite regulatory changes, client insourcing via Global Capability Centres (GCCs), and technological shifts in enterprise software delivery. All figures studied in the Learning Lab rely on delayed reported filings and must be verified against official exchange disclosures.
